    AI in safety management programs

    What safeguards should safety professionals look for before trusting that artificial intelligence-generated guidance is accurate enough to act on?

    By S+H Staff
    September 18, 2026
    Share
    Facebook
    X
    Linkedin
    Email

      Responding is Alex Sadovsky, chief AI officer, Enhesa, Brussels.

      Listen to audio version of this article
      Sponsored by
      0:00 / 3:13
      Instaread

      Safety professionals are well practiced at distrusting confidence with nothing behind it. A contractor who waves off a permit. A checklist signed but never checked. Now there’s a new one: the generic AI tool that answers instantly and fluently, whether or not it’s right.

      The principle is simple: The model is never the source of truth, only the fastest route to it. Every safeguard follows from that, and each has a test you can run.

      Where did this come from? There’s a real difference between a system that cites the clause behind its answer and one that generates a plausible blend from a training set. Ask whether the citation points to the regulation itself or a vendor’s summary; summaries of summaries drift. Then ask it something it can’t possibly know. You want to hear, “I don’t have coverage for that jurisdiction.” A tool that always answers confidently will eventually answer confidently wrong.

      As of when? Regulations change, enforcement priorities shift and a model is a snapshot of its training date. A correct answer for 2024 is a wrong answer for 2026. Every answer should carry the version it drew on and its effective date. Then ask the provider how long a published change takes to appear, and who’s accountable for that. If nobody can name that person, the content isn’t maintained, it’s hosted.

      Does this actually apply to my operation? Obligations sit buried in a document, cross-referenced into another regulation, or layered across national and subnational requirements a surface reading misses. Finding them takes subject matter expertise built into the content, not a model reading text it’s never seen. Ask how applicability is determined, and what the system needs to know about your sites, processes and substances to determine it.

      Could I defend this to an auditor? If a regulator or auditor asks how a decision was reached, “The AI told us” isn’t an answer. You need a traceable line from the guidance back to a verified source, plus a record of who reviewed it and when. No log, no defensible decision. Then run your own test: 20 questions from your operations where you know the answer, three where the honest answer is “it depends,” and two where no requirement exists at all. Score them yourself.

      The same issue underlies all four questions. AI can chew through regulatory volume and draft a strong first pass faster than any team of people. It’s genuinely useful, and safety leaders should be using it for exactly that. What it can’t do is stand in front of an auditor, be named on a corrective action or lose a license over a bad call. A qualified human has to own the interpretation.

      Skip that step and you’ve handed judgment to something that can’t be held responsible. Before acting on AI-generated guidance, answer four things: where it came from, how current it is, whether it applies to you and whether you could defend it.

      What makes AI trustworthy isn’t the answer; it’s the accountability behind it.

      Editor’s note: This article represents the independent views of the author and should not be considered a National Safety Council endorsement.
